summary: RFC 7854 defines the BGP Monitoring Protocol with several message types, many using TLVs. The Peer Up message shared a namespace with the Initiation message, which hampers extension. This document gives Peer Up its own namespace.

eli5.summary: Two kinds of messages were sharing one list of labels, which got confusing. This gives each its own list.

questions: what is the bmp peer up message
what is a bmp peer up information tlv
what changed in rfc 7854 for peer up
what is the bmp vrf table name tlv
subtitle: BMP gives the Peer Up message its own list of TLV types instead of sharing one with the Initiation message.

tldr.problem: In the BGP Monitoring Protocol, the Peer Up message and the Initiation message shared one namespace of Information TLV types. Experience showed this hampers extending the protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC renames the shared TLV to the Initiation Information TLV and defines a separate Peer Up Information TLV with its own IANA registry, holding String (0), VRF/Table Name (3) and Admin Label (4).
tldr.outcome: Each message can now grow new TLV types independently. The RFC updates RFC 7854, RFC 8671 and RFC 9069, and says compliant implementations of those RFCs also comply with it.

today: RFC 9736 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025. It updates RFC 7854, RFC 8671 and RFC 9069, and no later RFC is recorded as updating or obsoleting it.

sections.title: Why the Namespaces Needed Splitting
sections.content:
RFC 7854 defines the BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP) and its message types. Apart from Route Monitoring, these messages are structured as Type, Length, Value (TLV). Most message types have their own namespace and IANA registry.

The Peer Up message was the exception: its namespace overlapped that of the Initiation message. As BMP was extended, the overlap became problematic. This RFC creates distinct namespaces for the two messages to remove it.

The RFC also states that compliant implementations of RFC 7854, RFC 8671 and RFC 9069 also comply with this specification.
sections.eli5: Imagine two clubs using one list of badge colors. Whenever one club wanted a new color, the other club was affected too. Now each club gets its own list.

sections.title: The String TLV
sections.content:
The RFC adds one small definition used by both messages. A string TLV is a free-form sequence of UTF-8 characters whose length in bytes is given by the TLV's Length field.

There is no requirement to end the string with a null or any other particular character, because the Length field gives its end.
sections.eli5: A string TLV is just a piece of text with a number in front saying how long it is, so you know where it stops.

sections.title: Changes to the Initiation and Peer Up Messages
sections.content:
The Information TLV from RFC 7854 is renamed the Initiation Information TLV. It is used only by the Initiation message, not by the Peer Up message. Type 0 is redefined as a String whose value is administratively assigned. If several string TLVs are included, their order MUST be preserved when they are reported. Type 1 (sysDescr) and Type 2 (sysName) are unchanged and must equal the matching MIB-II objects.

The last paragraph of the Peer Up Notification section in RFC 7854 is replaced. The Information field now uses the new Peer Up Information TLV format. The String type may be repeated, including the field is OPTIONAL, and its presence can be inferred from the Message Length in the common header.
sections.eli5: The old shared label list is renamed so it belongs only to the Initiation message. The Peer Up message is told to use its new list, and it may leave the notes out entirely.

sections.title: The Peer Up Information TLV
sections.content:
The new TLV has a 2-byte Information Type, a 2-byte Information Length (the length of the Information field in bytes) and a variable Information field. Types come from the new "BMP Peer Up Message TLVs" registry.

  • Type 0, String: an administratively assigned string. If several are included, their order MUST be preserved when reported.
  • Type 3, VRF/Table Name: a UTF-8 string that MUST equal the VRF or table name being conveyed (for example an RD instance name). Its size MUST be 1 to 255 bytes.
  • Type 4, Admin Label: a free-form, administratively assigned UTF-8 string whose byte length is given by the Information Length field.
sections.eli5: Each note on a Peer Up message says what kind of note it is, how long it is, and then gives the note. The kinds are a plain note, the name of a routing table, and a label chosen by the network operator.

sections.title: The New and Renamed Registries
sections.content:
IANA created the "BMP Peer Up Message TLVs" registry and renamed the old "BMP Initiation and Peer Up Information TLVs" registry to "BMP Initiation Information TLVs". The new registry has these ranges: 0 and 3 to 32767 by Standards Action, 32768 to 65530 First Come First Served, 65531 to 65534 Experimental, and 1 to 2 plus 65535 Reserved.

In the Peer Up registry, types 1 and 2 are reserved because they mean sysDescr and sysName only in the Initiation message. In the renamed Initiation registry, types 3 and 4 are reserved so the two lists do not clash.
sections.eli5: The official list keeper made a new list for Peer Up and renamed the old list. Numbers that mean different things in each list are blocked off so nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC does not alter the security considerations of RFC 7854, which continue to apply. It adds no new security mechanism.
sections.eli5: Nothing about safety changes. The same rules as before still apply.
